records.name: Decision quality chain

origin.author: Carl Spetzler, Hannah Winter, Jennifer Meyer

records.summary: A good decision has six links: an appropriate frame, creative alternatives, relevant information, clear values and trade-offs, sound reasoning, and commitment to act. The weakest link sets the quality.
records.key_question: Which of the six links in this decision is weakest?
use_when: what are we missing before we decide
records.produces: a rating of the six links with the weakest one named and what would strengthen it
records.failure_mode: Rating every link as strong because the preferred option is already chosen.

records.name: WRAP
records.summary: Widen your options, reality-test your assumptions, attain distance before deciding, prepare to be wrong. Each step targets a documented decision bias.
records.key_question: Which of widen, reality-test, distance or prepare have I skipped?
records.produces: a decision record with widened options, reality checks, a distanced view and a plan for being wrong
records.failure_mode: Running the four steps as a checklist after the choice is already made.
steps: Widen your options: add at least one option beyond the current either/or.
Reality-test your assumptions: look for disconfirming evidence and small experiments.
Attain distance: ask what you would advise a friend and how you will see it later.
Prepare to be wrong: set tripwires and a range of outcomes.

records.name: Vanishing options test
records.summary: Imagine every option currently on the table is forbidden. What would you do then? Exposes options that narrow framing hid.
records.key_question: If none of my current options were allowed, what would I do?
use_when: should I do this or not
I can't see any other choices
records.produces: new options found after imagining the current ones forbidden
records.failure_mode: Generating only small variants of the forbidden options.
steps: List the options currently on the table.
Imagine every one of them is no longer possible.
Ask what you would do instead and write at least three answers.
Add the strongest new options to the list.

records.name: Expected value
records.summary: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add them up. Shows which option is best on average, and makes the probabilities you are assuming explicit.
records.key_question: What is each option worth on average, and which probabilities am I assuming?
use_when: which option pays off on average
records.produces: a table of outcomes, probabilities and payoffs per option with the expected value of each
records.failure_mode: Using made-up precise probabilities and treating the result as settled; ignoring ruinous tails.

records.name: Decision tree
records.summary: Map choices, chance events and outcomes in sequence and roll back from the end. Separates what you control from what you do not and shows when later information changes the best first move.
records.key_question: Which choices come later, after I learn something?
use_when: what happens if I choose this and then
map out the scenarios and choices
should I wait for more information
records.produces: a tree of choices and chance events with values rolled back to the first move
records.failure_mode: Leaving out the chance branches you would rather not think about.
steps: Write the first decision and its options as branches.
After each option, add the chance events that could follow, with probabilities.
Add later decisions where you will choose again.
Assign a value to each end point.
Roll back from the end: average over chance nodes, take the best at decision nodes.

records.name: Weighted criteria
records.summary: Name the criteria, weight them before scoring, score each option, sum. The value is in the weighting conversation; the total is only as good as the weights.
records.key_question: Did I set the weights before I saw the scores?
records.produces: a scoring table with weights set before scoring, totals, and a sensitivity check on the weights
records.failure_mode: Adjusting weights after scoring until the preferred option wins.
steps: List the options.
Name the criteria that matter.
Assign weights before looking at scores.
Score each option on each criterion.
Multiply and sum.
Check whether a reasonable change in weights changes the winner.

records.name: Even swaps

origin.author: John Hammond, Ralph Keeney, Howard Raiffa

records.summary: Trade one criterion for another until two options are equal on it, then drop that criterion. Repeat until dominance settles the choice. Avoids arbitrary weights.
records.key_question: What would I give up on one criterion to gain on another?
records.produces: a reduced comparison where criteria were eliminated by swaps until one option dominates
records.failure_mode: Making swaps that are not truly equal in value to you.
steps: Build a table of options against criteria.
Remove any option that is dominated by another.
Pick a criterion and adjust one option's score to match another's, compensating on a second criterion.
Once a criterion is equal across options, drop it.
Repeat until one option dominates.

records.name: Value-focused thinking
records.summary: Start from what you value, not from the options available. Options built from values beat the best of the given menu.
records.key_question: What do I actually want, before I look at what is on offer?
use_when: none of these options feel right
what matters most to me here
records.produces: a list of the values at stake and new options built from them
records.failure_mode: Listing values that are really features of the options already on the table.

records.name: Scenario planning

origin.author: Pierre Wack; Peter Schwartz
origin.work: Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead (HBR); The Art of the Long View

records.summary: Pick the two most uncertain and most important drivers, cross them into four plausible futures, and test each option against all four. The aim is robustness, not prediction.
records.key_question: Does this option survive in all four futures, or only the one I expect?
use_when: the future is too uncertain to plan
records.produces: four scenarios from two crossed uncertainties, with each option rated for robustness across them
records.failure_mode: Picking drivers that are uncertain but unimportant, or important but predictable.
steps: List the drivers that will shape the outcome.
Pick the two that are most uncertain and most important.
Cross them to make four futures and name each.
Write a short story for each future.
Test each option in all four; prefer the one that holds up across most.

records.name: Reference-class forecast

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman & Dan Lovallo; Bent Flyvbjerg
origin.work: Timid Choices and Bold Forecasts; From Nobel Prize to Project Management

records.summary: Forecast from the outcomes of similar past cases (the outside view) first, then adjust for what is genuinely different about this case.
records.key_question: How did similar cases actually turn out?
records.evidence_note: Planning-fallacy correction with strong field evidence in large projects (Flyvbjerg). Depends on choosing the right reference class.
use_when: how long will this really take
what usually happens in cases like this
records.produces: a forecast starting from the outcomes of similar cases, with the adjustments made and why
records.failure_mode: Choosing a reference class so narrow it contains only success stories.
steps: Identify a class of similar past cases.
Find the distribution of their outcomes.
Place your case in that distribution as a starting estimate.
Adjust only for differences you can name and justify.
Keep the adjustment small unless the evidence is strong.

records.name: Pre-mortem
records.summary: Imagine it is a year later and the decision failed. Write why. Imagined certainty of failure frees people to name risks they would otherwise keep quiet.
records.key_question: If this has failed a year from now, what is the most likely reason?
records.evidence_note: Prospective hindsight increased the number of reasons generated by about 30% (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989). Effect on decision outcomes less studied.
use_when: what could go wrong with this
records.produces: a list of reasons the decision failed, ranked, with a mitigation for the top ones
records.failure_mode: Writing generic risks instead of specific stories of failure.
steps: Assume it is a year later and the decision has failed badly.
Everyone writes the reasons it failed, independently.
Pool the reasons and remove duplicates.
Rank by likelihood and impact.
Add mitigations or kill criteria for the top reasons.

records.name: Keep options open
records.summary: When a decision is irreversible and uncertainty will resolve, waiting or staging has value. Buy the right to decide later with a small first step.
records.key_question: What small step buys me the right to decide later with better information?
use_when: should I wait or commit now
can we keep our options open
records.produces: a staged plan with the small first step, what it buys, and when the full decision will be made
records.failure_mode: Using delay as avoidance when uncertainty will not actually resolve.

records.name: Value of information
records.summary: Information is worth paying for only if it could change the decision. If no plausible answer would change what you do, stop researching and decide.
records.key_question: What could I learn that would actually change my choice?
use_when: should I research more before deciding
records.produces: for each open question, whether any plausible answer would change the decision
records.failure_mode: Researching questions whose answers would not change the choice.

records.name: One-way and two-way doors
records.summary: Reversible decisions should be made fast and by few people; irreversible ones slowly and carefully. Most decisions are reversible and are treated as if they were not.
records.key_question: If this goes wrong, can I walk back through the door?
use_when: how carefully should I decide this
records.produces: the decision classified as reversible or not, with the matching speed and number of people
records.failure_mode: Treating an irreversible decision as reversible because it is convenient.

records.name: Explore or exploit

origin.author: Multi-armed bandit theory; Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths

records.summary: Explore while you have a long horizon left, exploit what you know works as the horizon shortens. Optimal stopping gives a rough rule for when to stop searching.
records.key_question: How much time is left to benefit from exploring further?
use_when: should I keep looking or settle
try new things or stick with what works
how many options should I see
records.produces: a statement of the horizon left and whether to explore or exploit now, with a stopping rule
records.failure_mode: Exploring indefinitely because the horizon is never stated.

records.name: Decision versus outcome
records.summary: Judge a decision by the information and reasoning available at the time, not by how it turned out. A good outcome can follow a bad decision.
records.key_question: Would I make the same call again with only what I knew then?
use_when: it went wrong so we chose badly
records.produces: a review separating the quality of the decision from the quality of the outcome
records.failure_mode: Using the outcome as the main evidence about the decision.

records.name: Kill criteria
records.summary: Before committing, write the conditions and the date at which you will stop. Decided in advance, quitting does not depend on willpower in the moment.
records.key_question: What would have to happen, by when, for me to stop?
use_when: how will I know to stop
I keep throwing good money after bad
records.produces: written conditions and a date at which the commitment will be stopped
records.failure_mode: Kill criteria so loose they will never trigger.
steps: Write what you are committing to.
Write the signals that would show it is not working.
Turn each signal into a measurable condition.
Set a date to check.
Tell someone who will hold you to it.

records.name: Satisfice

origin.author: Herbert Simon; Barry Schwartz
origin.work: A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice; The Paradox of Choice

records.summary: Set the bar for 'good enough' and take the first option that clears it. Maximising across many options costs time and tends to lower satisfaction with the choice.
records.key_question: What is good enough, and does an option already clear it?
records.evidence_note: Maximizers report lower satisfaction (Schwartz et al. 2002); later replications show the effect depends on how maximizing is measured.
use_when: I can't choose between so many options
stop looking for the perfect one
records.produces: the 'good enough' bar written down and the first option that clears it
records.failure_mode: Setting the bar after seeing the options, so it fits the favourite.

records.name: Independent judgments first

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony, Cass Sunstein

records.summary: Break the decision into separate assessments, have each made independently before discussion, and combine them at the end. Reduces both noise and anchoring on the first opinion voiced.
records.key_question: Were the assessments made independently before anyone discussed them?
records.evidence_note: Mediating assessments protocol; aggregation of independent judgments is well supported (wisdom-of-crowds literature).
records.produces: independent assessments per dimension, recorded before discussion, and their combination
records.failure_mode: Letting people see each other's ratings before making their own.
steps: Break the decision into separate dimensions to assess.
Have each person rate each dimension independently and in writing.
Collect all ratings before any discussion.
Discuss the largest disagreements.
Combine the ratings using a rule agreed in advance.

records.name: Fear-setting
records.summary: Define the worst case in detail, how to prevent it, how to repair it; list the benefits of partial success; then the cost of not acting in six months, one year, three years.
records.key_question: What does inaction cost me over the next three years?
use_when: I'm scared to make this change
what's the worst that could happen
records.produces: a written worst case with prevention and repair, the benefits of partial success, and the cost of inaction over time
records.failure_mode: Listing fears without writing how to prevent or repair each.
steps: Define the worst outcomes in detail.
For each, write how to prevent it.
For each, write how to repair it if it happens.
Write the benefits of even partial success.
Write the cost of not acting at six months, one year and three years.

records.summary: How will I feel about this in ten minutes, ten months, ten years? Separates the short-term emotion from the long-term consequence.
records.key_question: How will this look in ten minutes, ten months and ten years?
use_when: how will I feel about this later
records.produces: three answers: how you will feel in ten minutes, ten months and ten years
records.failure_mode: Answering the ten-year question with today's feelings.
steps: State the decision.
Ask how you will feel about each option in ten minutes.
Ask the same for ten months.
Ask the same for ten years.
Note where the answers diverge and weigh the longer horizons.

records.name: Regret minimisation

origin.author: Jeff Bezos
origin.work: Interviews on leaving D. E. Shaw (1994)

records.summary: Project yourself to age eighty and ask which choice you would regret not having made. Useful for bold choices; biased toward action.
records.key_question: At eighty, which choice would I regret not having made?
use_when: will I regret not doing this
what would my older self think
records.produces: the choice you would regret not having made, viewed from late in life
records.failure_mode: Using it for decisions where caution matters more than boldness.

records.name: Fast and frugal heuristics

origin.author: Gerd Gigerenzer & Daniel Goldstein
origin.work: Reasoning the Fast and Frugal Way (Psychological Review)

records.summary: In uncertain environments, simple rules that use one good cue can match or beat complex models. Choose on the most important reason; stop when it discriminates.
records.key_question: What is the single most important reason, and does it already decide this?
records.evidence_note: Take-the-best matched or beat regression in out-of-sample prediction in several domains (Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996; Czerlinski et al. 1999).
use_when: what's the one thing that matters
records.produces: the one cue chosen and the decision it gives
records.failure_mode: Using a simple rule in an environment where the cue does not predict well.

records.name: Recognition-primed decision
records.summary: Experts match the situation to a pattern, simulate the first plausible action and take it if it works. Trust it where you have real experience with fast feedback, not elsewhere.
records.key_question: Do I have real experience with fast feedback in this kind of situation?
records.evidence_note: Naturalistic studies of firefighters and commanders (Klein 1998). Valid only where the environment is regular and feedback is quick (Kahneman & Klein 2009).
use_when: should I trust my experience here
records.produces: the pattern matched, the first action simulated, and whether your experience is valid in this domain
records.failure_mode: Trusting intuition in a domain without fast, clear feedback.

records.name: Body signal
records.summary: Emotional and bodily signals carry learned information about past outcomes and help narrow options. Treat the feeling as data to examine, not as a verdict.
records.key_question: What is my body telling me, and what experience could that signal come from?
records.evidence_note: Somatic marker hypothesis; the supporting Iowa Gambling Task evidence is contested (Dunn, Dalgleish & Lawrence 2006). Use as a prompt, not as evidence.
use_when: this feels wrong but I can't say why
I have a bad feeling about this
my body is telling me something
records.produces: the feeling named and examined for what past experience it might be signalling
records.failure_mode: Treating the feeling as a verdict instead of as data to examine.

records.name: Coin-flip gut check

origin.author: Piet Hein; Mariela Jaffé et al.
origin.work: A Psychological Tip (grook); Flipping a coin to decide (study)

records.summary: Assign each option to a side of a coin and flip it. The relief or disappointment you feel when it lands reveals the preference you already had.
records.key_question: When the coin landed, was I relieved or disappointed?
records.evidence_note: Coin flips helped people identify their preference and increased decision confidence (Jaffé, Reutner & Greifeneder 2019). Single research group.
use_when: I can't decide between two options
records.produces: the reaction to the coin flip and the preference it reveals
records.failure_mode: Obeying the coin instead of noticing the reaction to it.
steps: Assign each option to a side of a coin.
Flip it.
Notice your reaction the moment it lands: relief or disappointment.
Write down the preference the reaction shows.
Decide, using the coin's result only as a prompt.

records.name: Advise a friend

origin.author: Ethan Kross & Igor Grossmann
origin.work: Boosting wisdom (J. Exp. Psychology); Solomon's paradox

records.summary: Describe the decision as if a friend faced it, or in the third person, and say what you would advise. Distance improves reasoning about one's own situation.
records.key_question: What would I tell a friend to do?
records.evidence_note: Self-distancing improved wise reasoning (Grossmann & Kross 2014). Replicated across several studies.
use_when: what would I tell a friend
I can't think clearly about my own situation
records.produces: the advice you would give a friend facing the same decision
records.failure_mode: Describing the friend's situation with details that make it easier than yours.
steps: Describe the situation as if a friend were facing it.
Use their name or the third person, not 'I'.
Write the advice you would give them.
Compare it with what you are inclined to do yourself.

records.name: Discernment
records.summary: Notice which option brings lasting peace and which brings agitation over several days; imagine advising a stranger; imagine looking back at the end of life. A values-and-feelings method from a religious tradition, usable without the faith.
records.key_question: Over several days, which option leaves me settled and which leaves me unsettled?
use_when: I want to decide in line with my faith
a life decision that matters deeply
records.produces: a record over several days of the consolation or agitation each option brings, plus the stranger and deathbed views
records.failure_mode: Deciding on a single day's mood instead of the pattern over several days.
steps: State the choice and set aside a few days for it.
Each day, imagine having chosen one option and notice whether you feel lasting peace or agitation.
Record what you notice.
Imagine advising a stranger in the same position.
Imagine looking back at the choice at the end of your life.
Choose the option the pattern points to.

records.name: Values alignment

origin.author: Steven Hayes (acceptance and commitment therapy)
origin.work: Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life

records.summary: Name your stated values, then check each option against them. The option you lean toward but that contradicts your values usually signals avoidance.
records.key_question: Which option moves me toward what I say I value?
use_when: I'm leaning toward this but something's off
align my choice with what I care about
records.produces: each option checked against your stated values, with any contradiction named
records.failure_mode: Listing aspirational values you do not actually act on.
steps: Write your three to five core values in your own words.
For each option, mark whether it supports or contradicts each value.
Look at the option you lean toward.
If it contradicts your values, ask what it lets you avoid.

records.name: Hell yeah or no
records.summary: For optional commitments: if it is not an enthusiastic yes, it is a no. Protects time for the few things that matter. Wrong for obligations and for decisions with no enthusiastic option.
records.key_question: Is this an enthusiastic yes, and if not, why is it not a no?
use_when: should I say yes to this
should I take on this project
records.produces: a yes or no based on whether the response is an enthusiastic yes
records.failure_mode: Applying it to obligations or to choices where no option is exciting.

records.name: Decision journal
records.summary: Write the decision, the options, what you expect to happen and how confident you are, before you know the result. The only reliable defence against hindsight bias.
records.key_question: What do I expect to happen, and how sure am I, written down now?
records.produces: a journal entry with the decision, options, expected outcome and confidence, written before the result
records.failure_mode: Writing the entry after the result is known.
steps: Write the decision and the date.
Write the options you considered.
Write what you expect to happen and how confident you are.
Write how you feel physically and mentally.
Set a date to review the entry against what happened.

records.name: Survival score

origin.author: Panta Rhei (original)
origin.note: Original to Panta Rhei; describe as such.

records.summary: After the attacks, rate how much of the idea survives on a 0–10 scale, with the rule: one fatal flaw caps the score at 3, regardless of how many strengths there are.
records.key_question: After the strongest attack, how much of this is still standing?
use_when: how much of this idea survives
score this plan after the critique
is this idea still worth pursuing
records.produces: a 0 to 10 survival score with the fatal flaw, if any, and the strongest surviving element
records.failure_mode: Averaging strengths and weaknesses so a fatal flaw is diluted.
steps: List the attacks that landed and those that did not.
Check whether any attack is fatal on its own.
If one is, cap the score at 3.
Otherwise rate from 0 to 10 how much of the idea survives.
Write the strongest surviving element and the weakest link.

records.name: Pre-commit update triggers
records.summary: Before seeing new evidence, state what result would move your estimate and by how much. Prevents re-reading any evidence as confirmation.
records.key_question: What result would make me change my mind, decided before I see it?
use_when: set criteria before seeing the results
I keep reading everything as confirmation
how should this new data change my view
records.produces: a pre-registered list of results and the size of the update each would cause
records.failure_mode: Writing triggers so vague that any result can be read as meeting or missing them.

records.name: Diverge, then converge

origin.author: J. P. Guilford; Alex Osborn
origin.work: The Nature of Human Intelligence; Applied Imagination
origin.note: Guilford coined divergent/convergent production; Osborn's deferred-judgment rule.

records.summary: Generate first with judgment switched off, evaluate afterwards in a separate pass. Mixing the two kills weak-but-promising ideas before they can be improved.
records.key_question: Am I judging ideas while I am still supposed to be producing them?
records.card: No judging for the next ten ideas. Write the bad ones too.
use_when: I keep shooting down my own ideas
we argue about ideas as soon as they are said
I want a big list first and a shortlist later
every idea gets criticised in the room
records.produces: two separated passes: an unjudged idea list, then a shortlist
records.failure_mode: The judging pass never happens and the unfiltered list is treated as the result.

records.name: Name the feeling first
records.summary: Putting a precise word to an emotion lowers its intensity. When a problem is charged, label the feeling before framing the problem, or the feeling frames it.
records.key_question: What exactly am I feeling about this, in one precise word?
records.evidence_note: Affect labeling reduced amygdala response (Lieberman et al. 2007). Effect replicated in several paradigms; self-help translation is extrapolation.
use_when: I'm too upset to think about this
records.produces: one or two precise words for the feeling, written before the problem is framed
records.failure_mode: Using a vague label like 'stressed' that names nothing specific.

records.name: What is in my control

origin.author: Epictetus; Stephen Covey
origin.work: Enchiridion; The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

records.summary: Sort every element of the situation into what you control, what you influence and what you neither control nor influence. Effort goes to the first two.
records.key_question: Which part of this is actually mine to act on?
use_when: I'm worrying about things I can't control
where should I focus my energy
everything feels out of my hands
records.produces: three lists: what you control, what you influence, what you do neither, with the next action for the first two
records.failure_mode: Putting other people's choices in the control column.
